transcript.text: Good morning. I'm doing a survey of shoppers in Broadbeach. Would you have a few minutes to spare to answer some questions?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Oh...erm...yes, I guess that would be ok.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Thank you very much. Everybody seems so busy today.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well actually I don't have loads of time, so...
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Oh yes, of course. It really won't take long. Could I start by taking your name please?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Martyn Leigh. Martyn's with a Y.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And is your family name spelt L-double-E?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: It's L-E-I-G-H.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Thank you. We don't actually publish your name or details. It just makes it easier for me to identify people when I look at all the results at the end.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I see.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And can I ask, how did you get into town today?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, normally I catch the bus, but I'm on my motorbike today because I'm going to work later.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And could you tell me what you're doing this morning, I mean, the reason for your trip into town?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I've just been to the hairdresser. You see, I have a job interview at the council in a few days.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Oh really! Well, good luck with that.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Thanks a lot. And now I'm on my way to buy a suit that I can wear to the interview. I don't actually own one at the moment!
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: OK. Is that everything you're planning to do in town?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Yeah. Well, I've got to go and pick up my laptop. It broke a couple of days ago so I took it to the shop to get it fixed. They had to order a spare part, but apparently it's ready for collection now. I can't wait to get it back.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I'm sure. I hate it when my technology breaks down. ...One more thing, it's Saturday today - is that when you like to do your shopping?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well it's more a question of when I'm free. If I'm free on a Monday, that's when I choose to come into town. The shops are less busy then, which I always prefer.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: So, I'd like to ask you a few more questions to get your views about shopping in Broadbeach, if that's ok.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Sure. What would you like to know specifically?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: What would you say you like best about the shops here?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I'd probably say it's the service you get wherever you go.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: OK. And what do you think about the range of shops in Broadbeach?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Oh you can get almost anything you want here.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And what about recent changes? What do you like and dislike about them? For example, there are a lot of new coffee shops now, are you enjoying them?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: No, there are too many of them. It's a shame as those places could be occupied by other kinds of shops.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: What would you like to see instead?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, I think we have enough clothing shops. But there's only one place that sells books at the moment. It'd be nice to have a choice, you know.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Right. And have you been to the new shopping centre outside Broadbeach yet, Martyn?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Yes, once or twice. It's not that far from where I live.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It's a very modern-looking building, isn't it?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Yes, and it's lovely. The glass roof is certainly impressive. But my favourite thing is the plants they've put around the building. They're amazing, and so big already.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And what about the entertainment facilities? Have you used any of them yet? Like the new cinema?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Nah, not yet. I can't see any advantage in having it there because the one in town is actually bigger.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: OK, well thank you so much for...
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Hello and welcome to this podcast telling you about our annual business exhibition.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: This year, as always, it will be full of the very best speakers, features and innovations.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Let me start by reading some feedback from James Craig, who's exhibited with us for the past two years.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: James says, 'I'm director of a company called TalkCon, which is an office phone system.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: The first year we exhibited, we had a stand in the Business Village, where we made a lot of useful contacts.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: We also used the Breakout area where people could sit down and relax, and try out our products, and due to popular request we used that again last year.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Last year we also sponsored the innovative Business Connections Zone where people could leave their contact details on a board to contact other companies, and that also effectively raised our corporate profile.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: We're hoping that in the coming exhibition we'll also have a presence in the Digital Marketing centre, which is clearly a key area for our company.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: And also maybe have our own Talkcon Zone, at some stage.' The exhibition's open from 8am to 11 pm and there's a range of special events for you to enjoy in the evening.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: As well as a unique chance to publicise your company, businesses who exhibit with us can claim discounts on a number of popular brands, including major high street fashion and jewellery outlets, as well as grocery chains.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Discounts available range from 3.5% up to an amazing 15%, so you can save a lot of money.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: In fact, the average saving made by each exhibitor came to over £400!
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: The scheme is available to every member of your organisation so this is a benefit that really does have something for you all.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Now let me tell you about some of our keynote speakers for this year's exhibition.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Jim Clowrie started off selling vegetables from a small plot, then opened a small café.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Rather to his surprise this became a bit of a sensation, and in a remarkably short time he had opened an amazing 76 restaurants worldwide.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: He'll be telling you how it all happened, and how it changed his life.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: David France will be giving an inspirational talk about how as a business-minded teenager he managed to set up his own company, and even to be the first person under 18 to get a business bank account.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: David's company has gone from strength to strength but he isn't just interested in making money -he also makes regular donations to organisations helping those in need both in the UK and elsewhere in the world.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Oliver Stanton was born and educated in the UK, and then went to Malaysia where he set up a rubber-wood furniture business.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: He then built log houses in the mountains in Japan before moving to Hong Kong to set up a digital marketing business.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: After that he moved back to the UK with his wife Saiphin, and together they opened a Thai café.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: He'll be telling you about what he discovered during his travels around the world about business practices in different cultures.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Francesca Heptonstall is a broadcaster and businesswoman who's known for her down-to-earth attitude.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: After winning a top job in a TV contest, she launched a number of online deal sites.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Her main business interest is in technology, but she's also passionate about helping people gain employment and organises an annual jobs fair, so she'll be concentrating on this in her talk.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Salman Khan is the Chief Executive of QBF Enterprises, and has turned around this business from a major publishing business to one of the UK's largest digital marketing service providers.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: He'll be talking about the need for flexibility to cope with new directions in today's business world.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Finally, Annie Craven is a consultant and coach who works with people to create lasting changes in their business and life.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Her session will offer an interactive look at different obstacles in people's own lives, not just in business.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: She also looks at how you can overcome them, whether you're starting out in business or at the top of your game.
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: Now let me ...
transcript.speaker: HOST

transcript.text: You know that joint presentation we've got to do this semester, Leo?
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: On houses of the future?
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: That's right. I'm a bit concerned - are we meant to come up with creative new suggestions for these houses?
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: I don't think so. It's more a matter of reporting and evaluating possible developments. But we mustn't be too general, we've got to support our points by referring to specific cases. So that'll need a lot of work.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: I'm afraid so. When's it got to be done by?
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: In about 6 weeks, so that's not too much of a rush.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: Good. We'd better decide now what type of housing we're going to focus on. How about housing for different generations living together?
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: We could do. Or accommodation for one person?
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: I think someone else is doing that. I was wondering about housing for the elderly? That's likely to become more important.
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: Yeah that's true. But I think your suggestion about intergenerational living might be more interesting -let's go with that.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: OK. Now I think the future demand is mainly going to be for accommodation in urban areas. So one way of meeting that demand might be to use existing commercial buildings and adapt them to form accommodation...
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: ... or come up with original ways of organising space so that people can live in smaller homes. But I think the solution is to design multi-storey apartment blocks.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: Building up rather than out, yes.
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: Let's think of some specific developments for houses of the future.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: OK. How about increased use of roof space on high-rise buildings for gardens.
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: Yes. In fact it doesn't have to be high-rise, you can do it on a one-storey building in a suburb, but it would greatly improve how you feel if you live in an urban high-rise.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: Especially if you don't have a balcony.
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: Yes. I think homes of the future will all need access to a shared working space, somewhere in the same building or group of houses, where people can go and work instead of just having a laptop on the kitchen table.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: Yes, so they aren't having to travel to an office but can still interact with others. That's often how new ideas get generated - by chatting to someone from a different profession.
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: Yeah. I read about a type of design where the internal walls of an apartment are moveable, so the space can be adapted over time as people's needs change. Like when children leave school and start working but still continue to live with their parents for many years? Or when an elderly relative moves in with the family... it would mean they could still have their own space, specially designed for their needs.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: Yes. Have you heard about those smart bathroom mirrors which can monitor people's health? They recognise signs of illness and contact a doctor automatically?
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: Hmm, not so sure they're a good idea.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: Nor am I. People might worry about conditions which aren't serious at all.
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: What about transport? Wouldn't it be good if there were bike sheds with charging points, so people could store their electric bikes securely and charge them up at the same time.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: Yes. That would encourage more people to cycle, instead of using their car. Much better for the planet.
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: I read about one housing development where cars had to be left just outside it, so the centre was all a pedestrianised area. Great for families with children.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: Maybe. But what if you're disabled or elderly, and can't walk far? It wouldn't be so good for people like that.
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: No.
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: I saw a scheme for communal vegetable plots, where neighbours could decide what to grow together. That'd be a great way for older people to get to know one another, especially if they're no longer going out to work.
transcript.speaker: MIA

transcript.text: Yes, doing something together's always more enjoyable, isn't it? Do you think...
transcript.speaker: LEO

transcript.text: Today's lecture is about studies that look at how music therapy can be used to help patients who undergo surgery.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Now, most people undergo a surgical procedure at some point in their lives.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And more than fifty-one million operations are performed annually in the USA.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But there's no escaping the fact that most patients feel uncomfortable following surgery.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They may have difficulty mobilising, and even sitting up in bed can feel too much.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They may also be negatively affected by having their routine disturbed, you know, like if they can't do the things they normally do, or have to devote a lot of time to appointments such as physiotherapy, to aid their recovery.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Currently, the main strategy for improving recovery is medication to control pain, and this can be administered to patients in the short, medium or longer term, depending on the extent of their surgery.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But music is still not an everyday part of the post-surgical phase, despite a wealth of relevant studies supporting its potential in recovery.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Earlier this year, a research team set out to assess all the available evidence so that they could highlight the potential for music in surgical recovery.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They identified nearly a hundred trials involving a total of seven thousand patients who were played recorded music as part of their post-operative care.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The researchers then looked at what impact the music had on the patients.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They discovered that patients who had been played music reported feeling happier and more satisfied in the post-operative phase, and the length of their stay was shorter than for patients who had not listened to any music.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The researchers also explored the patients' choice of music, and their findings showed that a wide variety of music styles was evident.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, a common factor was that the chosen music had a calming quality.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some of the patients listened to music with headphones, but it was quiet enough not to prevent them from being able to communicate with nurses and other staff.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: More often though, the mode of delivery was by what are known as music pillows.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These broadcast sound that is only audible to the person lying on them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The research involved testing music before, during or after operations or a combination.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some patients listened to the music just once a day, while others had several episodes a day.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: When asked to report their experience of listening to music, surgical patients said that either they had no feelings of anxiety at any point, or those feelings were only slight.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Patients who hadn't listened to music, on the other hand, reported higher levels of dissatisfaction.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This feedback from all of the patients was then cross-checked against their medical notes.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And in every case, those who were given music to listen to didn't need as much medication to ease their pain as those patients who weren't played music.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The type of music, patient choice and timing, before, during or after the surgery didn't make much difference.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And it even worked when patients were played music under general anaesthetic, although the positive effects were greater when patients were awake.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: All the evidence suggests that music has a positive effect on post-operative patients, but it's not entirely clear how or why this is the case.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: A lot of people listen to music in daily life as a way to relax and forget their problems, but the researchers came to the conclusion that it worked on patients by distraction.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: I suppose it was something familiar and gave them something they could control.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The researchers say there is now sufficient research to demonstrate that music should be available to all patients undergoing operations.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They say patients should be able to choose what they'd like to listen to, and if they prefer, recordings taken from nature can be just as good as music.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Surgical teams may prefer patients to listen to music before the procedure or as soon as they arrive back onto the ward.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Clearly, there's more to learn about this area, and the team now plan to focus their next research on the most appropriate volume to play the music at.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And I look forward to reading the results of their study.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It will be interesting to see ...
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
